title: The captive girl (2 Kings 5:2–3)
hook: an Israelite servant girl points her master toward healing

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great general almost refused the plain instruction: getting down off the chariot. Today we go back to the person who sent him to the prophet at all.

She gets only a few lines. No name, no age, no words about her family. Raiding bands from Aram had gone into the land of Israel, and among what they carried off was a young girl. Now she works in a foreign house, waiting on the wife of the commander whose raiders took her. That commander is Naaman. Everything we heard yesterday, the chariots, the gifts, the river, begins with something this girl says to her mistress.
screen: `A FEW LINES, NO NAME.` → `CARRIED OFF BY RAIDERS.` → `SERVING IN NAAMAN'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy." Look at who she's talking about. My lord. The man whose soldiers took her from her home. And her wish is for him to be healed. The text doesn't tell us what she felt, whether she was afraid, or homesick, or angry. It doesn't explain her motives at all. It only gives us the sentence, and the sentence is generous. Then watch how far it travels. Word goes up the household: thus and thus said the maid from the land of Israel. It reaches the king of Aram, and he writes a letter to the king of Israel. Armies, kings and letters start moving, all because a servant girl spoke up. The king of Israel panics when he reads it, tearing his clothes: am I God, to kill and to make alive? The king doesn't think of the prophet. The girl did. She knew there was a prophet in Samaria, and she trusted he could help. Two more things stand out. She points away from herself; she claims no power, she simply knows where help can be found. And the story never mentions her again. No reward, no freedom, no thanks recorded. Naaman comes home healed, and the text has already moved on. But the healing began with one sentence from someone with no power at all, and the text bothered to keep it.
screen: `WOULD GOD MY LORD WERE WITH THE PROPHET.` · `THE SENTENCE TRAVELS TO KINGS.` · then, large: `A SMALL GIRL'S WORD.` · then: `NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: This one is hard, so go gently: think of someone who hurt you in a small or middle-sized way, not the deepest wound, and without excusing what they did, ask the girl's question: is there one good thing I could wish for this person? Healing, rest, a better day; let the wish sit for a few breaths, and if it won't come, that's honest too. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers.
Na'arah ketanah. Hebrew for "a little maid," how the text describes a young Israelite taken by raiders, serving in Naaman's house, whose one sentence sent her master to be healed. Today's word.
Your line: a small girl's word. The smallest voice in the house knew where help was. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read the captive girl's words at the start of Naaman's story in the book of Kings, which is read in synagogue as a haftarah.

chat.meaning: The young captive wished her master well: would God my lord were with the prophet in Samaria. Her one sentence reached two kings.

Na'arah ketanah.meaning: a little maid, a young girl

Samaria.meaning: the capital city of Israel's northern kingdom

Aram.meaning: the kingdom whose raiders carried her off

Naaman.meaning: the commander of Aram's army, her master
